newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- JAN 21.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- JAN 21.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--The Athens Stock Exchange broke a three-year record yesterday, with the general price index closing 1,119.91 points, up 2.78 percent. Interest was centred once again on banking, with turnover exceeding 15 billion drachmas.

--There were concerns expressed over developments in public infolows and the achievenment of forecast targets at yesterday's meeting at the national economy ministry. The meeting confirmed that the state was already out by 200 billion drachmas in inflows in 1996.
--Private investors showed the main interest in yesterday's issue of two-year zero coupons, with sales reaching 230 billion drachmas.

--The continuing seamen's strike is causing considerable concern to markets as are threats by farmers to return to their positions on the nation's roads. The tourist sector in particular is apprehensive.

--The general price index reached its highest point since Febraury 1994 yesterday in a session characterised by intense buying interest across the board. Part of the reason for yesterday's rise, sources say, is foreign investment in blue chips.

--Reports say there are differences between ministers and OTE, Greece telecoms organisation, over whether financing for investment will come from a share capital increase or from another share offer. The percentage of OTE to be offered, sources say, is 10 percent.
--A Supreme Court justice yesterday intervened in the seamen's strike, calling for prosecution when illegalities are detected.
--Under the shadow of a week of strikes, the government is drafting the action plan for the execution of the 1997 budget. Additional measures to curb public spending are on the cards.

--The possibility of public utilities and organisations exceeding declared incomes policies is being greeted with serious concern in the government. The national economy secretary-general yesterday told a number of directors of services that wage increases could not exceed 7.0 percent, if inflation is to fall to 5.5 percent by end-1997.

--Tension continues to reign at the country's ports and the strike is developing into a serious problem for the economy. The market has also begun to worry about the farmers' threat to resume protests as their January 28 deadline nears.

--The mutual funds market in Greece has seen an increase of 1.8 trillion drachmas over the past half-year, and has shown an increase of 7.4 percent in the last 17 days alone, according to a new report. The market is now worth a total of 4.0 trillion drachmas.

--Economic issues take the spotlight this week as the new bill on public spending cutbacks is submitted to the parliament committee, probably tomorrow, and the plenum of the House starts discussion on the taxation bill on Thursday. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
